title: Harrdy Sandhu's New Single Debuts India's 72-Hour Subscriber-First Music Model
excerpt: 'Stuck On You' will be the first release under Universal Music India's subscriber-first window, giving paid streaming subscribers exclusive early access before the track goes wide.
body:
• Harrdy Sandhu's upcoming single 'Stuck On You' will be the first release under Universal Music India's new 72-hour subscriber-first window, launching on August 28 with wider availability from August 31.
  • The model gives paid subscribers on participating streaming platforms exclusive early access before songs reach ad-supported tiers — a first for India's music industry.
  • UMI says the initiative aims to strengthen the value of paid music subscriptions and build a more sustainable ecosystem for artists in India.
  • Sandhu, whose tracks like 'Bijlee Bijlee' and 'Kya Baat Ay' have massive global streaming numbers, remains one of the most popular Punjabi artists among the diaspora.

A New Release Model for Indian Music

Harrdy Sandhu's next single, 'Stuck On You,' will mark a first for India's music industry when it drops on August 28. The track, releasing via VYRL Originals, will be available exclusively to paid subscribers on participating streaming platforms for 72 hours before going wide across ad-supported tiers on August 31.

The release is the inaugural implementation of Universal Music India's (UMI) new subscriber-first release window — a strategy already familiar in Western markets but now being adapted for India's rapidly evolving streaming landscape. During the exclusivity period, only users with paid subscriptions on global and regional music services will be able to stream the track.

"I've always believed that the people who show up for your music should feel like they're a part of the journey. With 'Stuck On You,' I'm really excited that my fans who subscribe to these platforms will get to hear the song first."

— Harrdy Sandhu, Singer

Why the Subscriber-First Approach Matters

India's music streaming market has exploded over the past half-decade, but the vast majority of listeners remain on free, ad-supported tiers. Platforms like Spotify, JioSaavn, and Gaana have struggled to convert free users into paying subscribers at the rates seen in North America or Europe. UMI's new model is designed to change that equation by creating tangible, immediate value for the paying listener.

The initiative forms part of a broader strategy to strengthen paid subscription ecosystems while supporting what UMI describes as "a healthier and more sustainable music ecosystem." By giving paying subscribers first access to new releases from major domestic and international artists, the company hopes to demonstrate that a subscription is worth more than just an ad-free experience.

Beginning in late August, UMI plans to roll out the 72-hour window across releases from its roster of artists, starting with Sandhu. If the model gains traction, it could fundamentally reshape how new music is released and consumed in India.

Sandhu's Enduring Diaspora Appeal

The choice of Harrdy Sandhu as the inaugural artist is no accident. The Patiala-born singer and actor has built a fanbase that stretches well beyond India, with tracks like 'Bijlee Bijlee,' 'Kya Baat Ay,' and 'Naah' racking up hundreds of millions of streams globally. His music bridges Punjabi pop, Bollywood, and contemporary Hindi — a combination that resonates strongly with diaspora listeners in North America, the UK, and Australia.

Sandhu is also gearing up for his next Punjabi film, 'Ranjheya,' alongside Simrat Kaur and Angad Bedi, announced earlier this year. His dual career as a singer and actor has kept him consistently visible in both music and film industries.

For diaspora fans who already pay for streaming subscriptions, the 72-hour early access window is a straightforward benefit. For those in India still weighing the value of a paid plan, 'Stuck On You' may be the test case that tips the balance.

What Comes Next

UMI has signaled that the subscriber-first model will extend to other major releases in the coming months. The company has not disclosed which platforms are participating in the initial rollout, though global services like Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube Music, as well as Indian platforms like JioSaavn, are the likely candidates.

Whether India's largely free-tier streaming audience responds to the model will be closely watched by other labels and distributors. If 'Stuck On You' drives a measurable bump in paid subscriptions, the 72-hour window could become standard practice for major releases across the Indian music industry.
